questions.question: The description of a database's tables, columns and rules, without the data, is called its _____.
questions.explanation: The schema is the shape of the database; the rows inside are the data.

questions.question: Is it true that create_all can add a new column to a table that already exists?
questions.explanation: create_all only creates tables that are missing. It skips existing tables, so the new column never appears. Migrations are needed to change tables that already hold data.

questions.question: Why should every environment (laptop, tests, production) apply the same migration files?
questions.answer: So every database reaches exactly the same schema by the same steps.
questions.explanation: So every database reaches exactly the same schema by the same steps. Hand-made changes on one machine would make the databases drift apart and cause bugs that only appear in one place.

questions.question: Which two functions does every migration file contain?
questions.explanation: upgrade() applies the change and downgrade() undoes it. A sounds right in general, but those are not the names Alembic uses.

questions.question: Each migration names the one before it, which forms a _____ of revisions.
questions.explanation: The down_revision field points to the parent, so Alembic knows the order. The newest migration is the head.

questions.question: How does Alembic know which migrations a database has already run?
questions.answer: It reads the alembic_version table in that database, which stores the current revision id, and runs only the migrations after it.
questions.explanation: It reads the alembic_version table inside that database, which stores the current revision id. It then runs only the migrations that come after it in the chain.

questions.question: What does "alembic upgrade head" do?
options: Creates a new migration file from the models
Runs every migration not yet applied, up to the newest one
Deletes and recreates all the tables
questions.explanation: It applies the missing migrations in order and updates alembic_version. A is what "revision --autogenerate" does.

questions.question: Is it true that adding --sql to an upgrade prints the SQL without changing the database?
questions.explanation: This "offline" mode only shows the SQL, so you can check it (or give it to someone) before running it for real.

questions.question: Why must you read an autogenerated migration before running it?
questions.answer: Because autogenerate only guesses; a renamed column looks like drop + add, which would delete its data.
questions.explanation: Because autogenerate only guesses from differences. A renamed column looks like "drop the old column, add a new one", which would delete the data in it, so you fix it by hand.

questions.question: In SQLAlchemy 2, a column is declared with a type hint like _____[int].
questions.explanation: Mapped[int] tells SQLAlchemy (and your editor) that this attribute is a database column holding an int; without Optional it is NOT NULL.

questions.question: Is it true that ON DELETE CASCADE makes the database delete the child rows when their parent row is deleted?
questions.explanation: The database itself removes rows that point to the deleted one, for example a user's habits and their check-ins, so no orphan rows are left.

questions.question: A check-in table has a unique constraint on the pair (habit, day). What does it prevent?
options: Two habits with the same name
A habit having check-ins on two different days
A check-in that points to no habit
Two check-ins for the same habit on the same day
questions.explanation: The pair must be unique, so one habit can be checked only once per day. C is the job of the foreign key, not of the unique constraint.

questions.question: Why store the day a habit was done as a local date instead of a UTC timestamp?
questions.answer: Because what counts is the day in the user's own time zone; a late-evening check-in could land on the next day in UTC.
questions.explanation: Because what counts is the day in the user's own time zone. A check-in at 23:30 local time could fall on the next day in UTC; a plain date avoids that and makes "once per day" easy to enforce.

questions.question: Is it true that without a naming convention, you can always predict the names the database gives to constraints?
questions.explanation: Each database picks its own default names. A naming convention gives names like uq_users_email, so a later migration can find and drop the constraint by name.

questions.question: Why should tests build their database with the real migrations instead of create_all?
questions.answer: So the tests use the same path as production and a broken migration fails the tests, not the real server.
questions.explanation: So the tests use the same path as production. A broken migration (or a broken downgrade) then fails the tests instead of failing on the real server.

questions.question: A test compares the models with the migrated database. When does it fail?
options: When a model changed but no migration was written
When the test database has no rows
When a migration has a downgrade function
When the app has no users yet
questions.explanation: Any difference between models and migrated schema means a migration is missing. B is not a problem: the test compares the shape, not the data.
